## Deep read
The trap works because attention obeys the first wording it hears. Once the teen reader reads the problem as "break up or not," every fact starts serving that ballot. A sister's comment becomes evidence for leaving. A sweet text becomes evidence for staying. The relationship, the family pressure, and the timing all get flattened into one door.

Quaker's Snapple deal shows the same squeeze at corporate size. The Quaker executive studies a packet with Snapple on the cover and about $1.8 billion on the price line. The page says acquisition, but the deeper problem is growth. If the meeting treats Snapple as the growth plan, the group may argue valuation while skipping other paths.

Money makes the missing path easier to see. Opportunity cost is plain: every dollar, hour, or bit of attention used here cannot be used there. A price tag is also a mirror. It asks what else the same resources could do.

Two small tests help. First, listen for whether-or-not wording. Should we buy Snapple? Should the teen reader end it? That wording is a warning light, not a verdict. Second, make the visible options disappear for a moment. If this choice vanished, what would you try next? The test does not pick the winner. It makes the room less captive.

A bigger frame is not a bigger mess. Wider does not mean endless. It means at least one more real path before judgment begins. You cannot compare what you never allowed on the table.

## Examples
### Example 1: The Phone-Screen Ballot
Tags: claireabelle, relationship, whether-or-not
After dinner, Claire writes under the handle claireabelle from a bedroom floor, phone balanced on a quilt. The post names a teen relationship, family interactions, and one visible question: break up or not. No one has moved yet. The tiny cursor after the question is doing the narrowing work.

What to do: Claire underlines the break-up-or-not wording, then writes two missing questions in the margin: what needs repair with the partner, and what boundary belongs with family.

Why it matters: The pause keeps a personal choice from becoming a false ballot. When the first wording shrinks the problem, the reader can widen it before feelings harden.

### Example 2: Snapple At The Table
Tags: Quaker, Snapple, acquisition
In a Quaker strategy room, the Quaker executive taps the Snapple packet beside the deal binder. "Snapple is the growth answer," he says. The strategist keeps his pencil on the $1.8 billion line. "Or it is one answer," he says. "If growth is the job, what else buys growth with this much money?"

What to do: The Quaker executive changes the meeting question from "Should Quaker buy Snapple?" to "What are the growth paths this money could fund?" The deal becomes one path.

Why it matters: The exchange moves the group from advocacy to comparison. A large acquisition should beat other growth paths, not merely sound bold inside its own frame.

### Example 3: Quaker Memo Catch
Tags: Quaker, Snapple, opportunity cost
The memo writer's Quaker memo has three pages on Snapple and no page for anything else. Her cursor blinks after the phrase "recommended acquisition." She notices the mistake before the printer warms: the $1.8 billion line has no rival use beside it.

What to do: The memo writer inserts an opportunity-cost page before the recommendation. She lists what the same capital could fund and marks which options also answer the growth need.

Why it matters: The correction happens before the argument gathers speed. Opportunity cost makes the hidden alternative visible while there is still time to compare.

### Example 4: Vanishing Options Draft

The adviser's unsent draft to claireabelle starts with a heading: "If the break-up-or-not frame were off the table." Below it, he writes three lines for the teen relationship. Talk to the partner about the family interactions; set one family boundary; wait until the fight is not fresh.

What to do: The adviser sends the Vanishing Options Test, not a verdict. He gives claireabelle a way to search for options before choosing among them.

### Example 5: Two Growth Lists
Tags: Quaker, Snapple, both-and
One strategist fills one column with reasons Quaker should buy Snapple. Another strategist writes a different page: acquire, partner, improve distribution, or test smaller brands. One strategist's page makes the acquisition feel inevitable. Another strategist's page makes the $1.8 billion choice compete.

What to do: One strategist tests the deal on its own terms. Another strategist tests the frame first, then asks which path solves growth with the least avoidable downside.

Why it matters: Both lists look serious, but only one creates comparison. A wide frame forces the visible option to earn its place against real alternatives.

### Example 6: Naming the Box

Q1. You hear a teammate ask only whether to approve one proposal. Which response best catches the narrow frame?
   a) Ask for stronger data on the proposal before anyone names other paths.
   b) Ask what problem the proposal solves and what other paths could solve it.
   c) Ask the team to vote quickly so the important option gets full attention.

Q2. A friend frames a family-stressed relationship as break up or stay. What should you notice first?
   a) The choice is personal, so widening it would only avoid the hard truth.
   b) The family conflict proves the relationship question has already been answered.
   c) The binary wording hides repair, boundary, timing, and support choices.

Q3. A manager treats one acquisition as the company's growth plan. Which reading fits the Quaker and Snapple warning?
   a) Big firms usually protect themselves by naming many real options first.
   b) A growth problem can shrink into one deal before other growth paths get compared.
   c) An acquisition is narrow only when the company pays too little to care.

Q4. A board packet shows Snapple at roughly $1.8 billion, and no other use of that money is listed. Why does the price matter?
   a) It shows the deal was too small to need a wider frame.
   b) It proves Quaker could safely treat the purchase as a quick test.
   c) It makes the missing alternatives costly because the commitment was large.

Q5. A project lead has two vendor bids taped to the wall, and every discussion returns to those names. How should the Vanishing Options Test be used?
   a) Remove both bids in thought and ask what the team would try next.
   b) Score both bids again until one becomes the automatic winner.
   c) Keep the cheaper bid and treat the test as a final selection rule.

Q6. A team fixing a late product says it must choose speed or quality before the next release. Which next question tests whether the tradeoff is real?
   a) Which side sounds more responsible to senior leaders right now?
   b) Which side has stronger defenders already in the meeting?
   c) What redesign would protect both aims before we decide one must lose?

Q7. A nonprofit board spends the whole agenda on whether to launch one new program, while staff time is already tight. What mistake would keep the frame narrow?
   a) They ask what need the program serves before reviewing the proposal.
   b) They spend the whole meeting making the single program easier to approve or reject.
   c) They name one other way to use the same staff time.

Q8. A director says a polished deal packet means the organization must have explored enough. What should a reader infer?
   a) A polished packet can still hide a one-option process.
   b) A polished packet proves the deal is no longer a narrow frame.
   c) A polished packet matters only when the company name is unfamiliar.

Q9. After using the Vanishing Options Test, what should happen next?
   a) Judge the expanded set, since the test creates options but does not pick among them.
   b) Accept the newest option, since anything found later is more creative.
   c) Return to the first option, since removing it was only a thought exercise.
